title: Supreme Court Rules Out Blanket Firecracker Ban, Warns Orders Must Not Become a Mockery
excerpt: A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale told the Delhi government and CAQM on Thursday that an absolute ban is no solution given festive enthusiasm — but demanded proof that its regulation orders are actually being enforced.
body:
• The Supreme Court said on Thursday it will not impose a complete ban on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR, citing festive sentiment, but also will not allow unrestricted use.
  • The bench pulled up the Delhi government and the CAQM for failing to show its earlier regulation orders are being implemented on the ground.
  • The Union government has been directed to file an affidavit on enforcement measures taken.
  • The court suggested using respected public figures, such as sportspersons, in awareness campaigns for a pollution-free Diwali.

The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled out an absolute ban on firecrackers, acknowledging the high festive enthusiasm around Diwali, but pulled up the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) for failing to demonstrate effective implementation of its earlier directions regulating firecracker use during the capital's winter festival-cum-pollution season.

A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale said the court understood the sentiment surrounding festivals but stressed that authorities must regulate firecracker use without causing harm to others. According to ANI's report of the hearing, the bench said it was not seeking an absolute ban, but wanted its existing directions effectively enforced, particularly on the days when firecrackers are permitted.

"Don't make a mockery of our orders"

The bench observed that its orders would become a "mockery" if the implementing mechanism was not put into operation on the ground, and directed the Union of India to file an affidavit on the enforcement measures taken, Verdictum reported. It said authorities could not simply proceed by filing cases against ordinary people celebrating a festival; the focus should be on ensuring regulatory directions are followed and the public is made aware of the consequences of firecracker use.

https://x.com/thenewsdrum/status/2115775232212656529

"Why can't you use the services of prominent personalities to make the public aware, like the sportsmen, or public figures who are highly respected, from any walk of life?"

— Supreme Court bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale

The balance the court has been drawing

Thursday's hearing continues the line the same bench set on September 30 in the long-pending Arjun Gopal v. Union of India matter, when it said it would neither agree to a total ban nor allow firecrackers to be used around the clock. A blanket prohibition, the court said then, could affect the sentiments of those celebrating the festival, while unrestricted bursting through the day would severely affect children, senior citizens, people who are ill and other living beings. The bench indicated it may permit specified categories of approved firecrackers during fixed time slots, and allowed joint firecrackers (ladis) subject to technical safeguards on manufacture, noise levels, shell size and the interval between bursts.

One question remains open: firecrackers containing barium. The court deferred that issue pending environmental testing, after the Centre sought more time to submit the Central Pollution Control Board's assessment of barium-based products.

What happens next

The Union's affidavit on enforcement is now the trigger document. Delhi's air typically deteriorates sharply in the weeks around Diwali, and a separate bench of the court warned this week that post-Diwali air quality in the capital will be very bad. For residents, the practical position going into the festival is unchanged in outline — regulated, timed use of approved crackers rather than a blanket ban — but the court has now put the burden squarely on governments to prove the rules are being enforced, not merely issued.
